title: Hillel on one foot
hook: asked to teach the whole Torah on one foot, Hillel says: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor, the rest is commentary, go and learn (Talmud, Shabbat 31a)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the swimmer went down with the swirl and came up singing: wu wei. Your line was go with the water. Where did you stop forcing? Day fifty-seven, and a new week: Jewish wisdom tales.

Somebody asks you to explain your whole job, your whole faith, your whole life's philosophy, in one sentence. Go. Right now. Elevator pitch. It's a slightly rude question, and a slightly brilliant one. Two thousand years ago, in Jerusalem, a man walked up to two of the greatest rabbis of his day with a version of it. The Talmud tells the story. He said: teach me the entire Torah, all of it, while I stand on one foot. The first rabbi, Shammai, chased him away. The second was Hillel. Today's story is Hillel on one foot.
screen: `EXPLAIN IT IN ONE SENTENCE.` → `TEACH ME ON ONE FOOT.` → `SHAMMAI, THEN HILLEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the scene, from the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Shabbat, page thirty-one. A man who isn't Jewish comes to Shammai and asks to be taught the whole Torah on one foot. Shammai, who is famously strict, pushes him away with the builder's measuring stick he's holding. So the man goes to Hillel, and asks the same thing. And Hillel doesn't send him away. He gives him an answer, in Aramaic, and it's short enough to say standing on one foot. What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah. The rest is commentary. Now go and learn. Three things happen in that answer. First, the center. The Talmud doesn't name a verse here, but many readers hear behind it the commandment in Leviticus, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society wording, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," put in its most practical form: don't do to others what you hate. You met a version of this on day four of this path, the golden rule, and it lives in many traditions. Second, the rest is commentary. Not unimportant, but built around that center. And third, the part people forget, the last words: now go and learn. Hillel doesn't say the one line is enough. He gives the summary, and then sends the man to study. The whole teaching fits on one foot. Living it takes two feet and the rest of your life. Hillel and Shammai, the Talmud says, often disagreed, and their schools argued for generations. Jewish tradition kept both sides of their arguments, and remembers Hillel especially for his patience.
screen: `SHAMMAI PUSHES HIM AWAY.` · `WHAT IS HATEFUL TO YOU, DON'T DO.` · `THE REST IS COMMENTARY.` · `THE ONE LINE ISN'T THE END.` · then, large: `NOW GO AND LEARN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand on one foot and say it. If you can, stand up now. If standing isn't right for you, sit tall and lift one hand instead. Find your balance. Say it quietly: what is hateful to me, I won't do to my neighbor. Wobble if you wobble. Then put your foot down, and breathe. Think of one person you'll see today, and one thing you'd hate someone to do to you, that you might be tempted to do to them. The bell holds the time.
Hillel on one foot. The whole Torah in one line: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. The rest is commentary; now go and learn. Today's word.
Your line: now go and learn. Today, live the one line once, on purpose. Then learn one new thing about something you thought you already understood. Day fifty-seven.

screen: `DAY 57 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HONI AND THE CAROB TREE.`

howItsDone: Jews study Hillel's answer in the Talmud, Shabbat 31a, and it is often taught to children as a first summary of Jewish ethics, always together with its last words: go and learn.

fork.setup: you're Hillel. a stranger asks you to teach the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. what do you do?
options: send him away, as Shammai did.
give him one line, and tell him to go and learn the rest.
tell him it can't be done.
fork.reveal: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. that is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. now go and learn.

original.note: Aramaic, zil g'mor: go, learn. Hillel's last words to the man on one foot.

trapdoor: what you thought: a clever rabbi's shortcut.
what it means: the center fits in one line, and living it takes a lifetime of study and practice.
what a scholar hears: Shabbat 31a, in Aramaic; many read it as Leviticus 19:18 put negatively and ends with zil g'mor, go and learn.

notes: Shabbat 31a paraphrased (Rodkinson/Soncino not quoted). The text's 'a gentile who came to convert' is rendered 'a man who isn't Jewish'; the script doesn't dwell on conversion. A Jewish Keeper may prefer to state the conversion context plainly.

Audit (second sample): the teach said Hillel 'takes the great commandment from Leviticus', a Gospel phrase and a link the Talmud passage never makes; it now says many readers hear Leviticus 19:18 behind his line, quoted from JPS 1917 (same wording as the KJV: confirm). Trapdoor adjusted to match.
Reference to day 4 of this path ('the golden rule') assumes that day's word; confirmed by the day-7 script's list of the week's words.
